title: AI Graveyard: Projects and Startups That Failed in 2026
summary: A comprehensive list of AI projects, startups, and products that shut down in 2026, from Character.ai's bankruptcy to OpenAI's failed super app redesign.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Over 42% of corporate AI initiatives fail due to funding issues, technical challenges, weak demand, or competition from larger platforms.
- Character.ai filed for bankruptcy in October 2026 after legal troubles and founder departures, with Disney bidding $20 million for its IP.
- Major players including OpenAI, Microsoft, and Apple have all rolled back or shut down high-profile AI products this year.


The AI industry's rapid growth has left behind a trail of ambitious projects that never made it. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, approximately 42% of corporate AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned due to insufficient funding, technical challenges, fierce competition, scaling difficulties, or weak user demand. This graveyard of failed ventures spans consumer apps, enterprise tools, and even products from the world's most valuable AI companies.


TechCrunch has compiled a comprehensive list of notable AI casualties from 2026, revealing that even industry giants are not immune to product failures and strategic missteps. The list serves as both a cautionary tale and a learning opportunity for the broader AI ecosystem.


## OpenAI's Failed Super App Experiment


On July 9, 2026, OpenAI attempted to transform ChatGPT into a unified super app by combining separate Chat, Codex, and Work modes while relegating the familiar interface to ChatGPT Classic. Users immediately criticized the redesign as confusing and cluttered, forcing OpenAI to roll back the changes shortly after launch.


The company has had better success with a different consolidation strategy: shutting down standalone products and folding their features into ChatGPT. ChatGPT Atlas, an AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before discontinuing on August 9, 2026. Similarly, Operator, an AI agent for web browsing and task completion, was absorbed into the main product. The company's video-sharing platform Sora shut down in March 2026 due to high operating costs and poor user retention.


## Character.ai's Dramatic Collapse


Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. The consumer chatbot app allowed users to interact with customizable bots modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. In 2024, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and rehire its founders, leaving the startup to continue without its leadership.


The company faced multiple lawsuits from families alleging its chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm. Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized character use. Despite barring under-18 users from open-ended chats and settling several suits with Google in early 2026, Character.ai filed for bankruptcy in October 2026. Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for licensing rights to some intellectual property. The sale is expected to conclude by late November or early December 2026.


## Hardware Failures and Privacy Scandals


The Humane AI Pin became one of 2026's most notorious hardware failures. After raising $230 million and generating significant hype, the wearable AI device struggled with poor performance and a dangerous battery fire risk in its charging case. Humane shut down the AI Pin business in February 2025, with HP acquiring most assets for $116 million.


The Rabbit R1, unveiled at CES in January 2024, sold 100,000 units initially but received harsh reviews describing it as unfinished with unreliable performance. The company continues updating the device and recently announced Project Cyberdeck, a portable device for vibe-coding applications.


Microsoft's Recall feature, announced at its 2024 Build conference, promised photographic memory for Windows PCs through automated screenshots. Privacy advocates immediately raised concerns about the security of sensitive data including passwords and financial information. Despite a nearly year-long delay and redesign, a cybersecurity researcher recently demonstrated how to extract Recall data, reviving fundamental privacy questions.


## Consumer App Shutdowns and Pivots


Several consumer-focused AI tools shut down in 2026 as larger platforms absorbed their functionality. Relay, a five-year-old workflow automation alternative to Zapier, closed entirely in August 2026 as OpenAI and Google built similar automation into their platforms. Ollie, a SOC 2-compliant family assistant app launched in June 2026, shut down on November 6 after failing to compete with established players like Muse and Instinct.


Huxe, built by former Google NotebookLM developers to convert text into podcast-style audio, closed in May 2026 as Spotify and other platforms expanded similar AI audio tools. Yupp, a free playground comparing responses from over 800 AI models while offering cryptocurrency rewards, shut down in March 2026 after failing to achieve product-market fit. Notion Mail, launched in April 2025, is scheduled to shut down on September 22, 2026, as users preferred separate AI agents for email management.


## Release Date


This comprehensive AI graveyard report was officially released on November 14, 2026, documenting the year's most significant product failures and strategic retreats across the artificial intelligence industry.


## What This Means


The growing AI graveyard demonstrates that market enthusiasm alone cannot sustain products without clear value propositions, manageable costs, and differentiation from platform giants. Startups face an uphill battle as companies like OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft absorb standalone features into their ecosystems. Privacy concerns, legal liability, and the challenge of monetizing free consumer AI products continue to pose existential risks. These failures provide critical lessons for the next generation of AI builders: focus on sustainable business models, address privacy and safety from day one, and identify use cases where specialized tools can outperform general-purpose platforms.
